newsitem.title: USA: Eli Lilly takes hit on PCS, downplays earnings impact.
newsitem.headline: Eli Lilly takes hit on PCS, downplays earnings impact.

text.p: Eli Lilly & Co. Monday faced up to a problem that Wall Street recognised years ago -- that the company paid way too much when it acquired its PCS Health Systems unit for $4.1 billion in 1994.
The Indianapolis-based drug giant announced it would take a $2.4-billion write-off on PCS, resulting in a charge against second-quarter earnings of $4.40 a share.
"Now that they've faced up to it and done what was expected, I think this issue will fade from view," said Principal Financial drug industry analyst Eugene Melnitchenko.

Combined with the recent sale of its stake in the Dow Elanco agricultural chemicals joint venture to Dow Chemical Co., Lilly's PCS write-off will yield a net increase in annual earnings of about 5 cents a share, it said.
The company told analysts not to raise earnings estimates, however, because it plans to plough gains from the bookkeeping adjustments into research and development and marketing.
Lilly said it is comfortable with analysts' 1997 earnings estimates in the $3.15 to $3.25 per share range, versus 1996 earnings of $2.78 per share on sales of $7.3 billion.
"They tried to put a good spin on it, linking it with the Dow Elanco deal," said Edward Froelich, drug industry analyst at the Pershing Division of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.
Investors still complained about Lilly's misjudgment on PCS in a teleconference Monday, analysts said.
"I didn't like this deal when they did it and I still don't. This reflects very poorly on them," one analyst said.
Fallout from the write-off is unlikely to stick to Lilly Chief Executive Randall Tobias, who engineered the PCS deal as one of his first acts in the Lilly head office, analysts said.
"All of the industry leaders were doing the same thing and (Tobias) probably concluded that he didn't want to be left out," Melnitchenko said.

PCS is a pharmaceutical benefits management concern that Lilly bought with the idea that it could be used to convince physicians to prescribe more Lilly drugs and to provide data needed for a broad push into "disease management."

Similar firms were acquired around the same time by Merck & Co. and SmithKline Beecham Plc, both major rivals of Lilly. PBM ownership has been profitable for Merck and SmithKline, while Lilly has seen much less benefit, mainly due to differences among the PBMs, analysts said.
Since the PCS deal, Lilly has nevertheless re-emerged as one of the world's top drug makers.
"Lilly was sort of fading when Tobias came in. He's revitalised everything. So his contributions have been much greater than" any problems PCS has posed, Melnitchenko said.

PCS is profitable, Lilly Chief Financial Officer Charles Golden said in a teleconference after Monday's announcement. "It's more profitable than it was a year ago and it's certainly a lot more profitable than it was two years ago. So we're growing in profitablity. We're clearly not where we want to be," he said.

Lilly sees future value in the unit, which counts among its customers such managed healthcare giants as Oxford Health Plans Inc. and the U.S. Federal Employee Health Benefit Programme, said Lilly spokesman Edward West.
At the time that Lilly acquired PCS, the company judged that it would be a greater risk not to do so, West said.
"The bad news is (PCS) didn't work out the way we'd anticipated. The good news is we were financially big enough to take that risk. And we would likely make the same decision again," West said.
Lilly stock fell $4.375 to $106 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
